# Vignette: Roberto

Roberto is a 65-year-old Latin American man who spent three years in military service in his early twenties, including a deployment that placed him in the middle of sustained ground combat. He watched men in his unit die. He carried a friend — barely twenty years old — off a hillside after an ambush, knowing before they reached the medic that the young man was already gone. Roberto never spoke about any of this when he came home. He married, found work, built a life. He told himself that was simply what you did.

For decades, the strategy more or less held. He became a special education teacher, working with children who had learning disabilities and behavioral challenges — kids who needed someone patient and steady, someone who didn't flinch. He was good at it. His students responded to him. He threw himself into the work with a kind of devotion that, if he is honest now, also served the purpose of keeping him too busy to sit quietly with himself. His marriage frayed over the years under the weight of his emotional distance, his difficulty being truly present, his tendency to go somewhere else in his mind even when he was physically in the room. His wife eventually left. He understood why, even as it devastated him.

The trouble that brought Roberto here began about two years ago, after he retired. Without the classroom to anchor him, the days became unstructured and the silence grew loud. He started sleeping poorly, waking at three or four in the morning with his heart pounding, the details of the ambush returning with a vividness that surprised and frightened him. He had assumed those memories had faded. They had not. They had simply been waiting.

Now he finds himself moving through the world with a low, persistent wariness he cannot entirely explain to himself. He sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He avoids the Fourth of July entirely — the fireworks send a spike of alarm through his body before his mind has time to catch up. He knows, intellectually, that he is in a suburban neighborhood and not a hillside, but his nervous system does not seem to have received that information. He describes a feeling of being permanently slightly braced, as though something is always about to happen.

He still volunteers two mornings a week at a local school, helping a young boy with dyslexia learn to read. He says this is the part of his week he looks forward to most. With the child, he is calm and focused, present in a way he struggles to be elsewhere. But on the drive home afterward, he sometimes finds his thoughts drifting back — to his friend's face, to the weight of carrying him, to the particular quality of light on that hillside. He will arrive home without remembering the last ten minutes of the drive.

Roberto does not describe himself as someone who suffers. He is matter-of-fact, even slightly apologetic, as though he worries about taking up too much space with his own history. He mentions, almost in passing, that he rarely talks to his adult children. Not because of any conflict, he says, but because he doesn't want them to see that something is wrong. He has spent forty years being the steady one, and he is not sure who he is if he isn't that.

What he does say, quietly, near the end of a session, is that he is tired. Not sleepy — though he is that too — but tired in a deeper way. Tired of managing something he has never named, tired of the vigilance, tired of the way the past keeps insisting on being present. He says he thought by sixty-five a man would have some peace. He is still waiting for it.
